title_original: Yaza Takenoshin Talks “Hinotama”, Family, Silence, Fantasy and Learning to Direct Through Space
excerpt_original: Yaza Takenoshin discusses “Hinotama”, Japanese family dynamics, fantasy, silence and turning space and movement into cinematic language.

blocks.text: Yaza Takenoshin Talks “Hinotama”, Family, Silence, Fantasy and Learning to Direct Through Space
Yaza Takenoshin discusses “Hinotama”, Japanese family dynamics, fantasy, silence and turning space and movement into cinematic language.

For Yaza Takenoshin, the premiere of “Hinotama: Ball of Fire” came with a particular kind of nervousness. Everything surrounding his first feature felt new, from working with experienced collaborators to presenting the completed film at a major festival. Yet nervousness had accompanied almost every stage of the production, to the point where the young filmmaker joked that he was gradually becoming accustomed to it.
Hinotama: Ball of Fire is screening at Busan International Film Festival

At the center of “Hinotama” is a 16-year-old boy living within a family that is gradually falling apart. He reconnects with a childhood friend he has not seen for eight years, and she tells him about a strange encounter with a ball of fire. Their search for this mysterious object becomes a means of escape, but fantasy eventually assumes a broader function within the film, helping connect the different fractures appearing inside the family.

One of Takenoshin’s main concerns was ensuring that the father did not become a straightforward villain. The character frequently behaves badly and says things that can make him easy to dislike, but the director wanted to understand where that behavior comes from. The family’s deterioration, in his view, cannot simply be attributed to one individual, while many of the father’s attitudes are also connected to the culture and social expectations in which he was raised. His words and behavior are recognizable as things that many Japanese men of his generation might say or believe.

Takenoshin is critical of some of those traditional values, particularly certain expectations surrounding etiquette and proper behavior, but he does not see direct criticism as his primary task. Instead, he wants to depict such attitudes precisely enough that audiences become aware of things they might hear every day without really noticing. Once familiar behavior is placed on a cinema screen and isolated from everyday routine, people can examine it differently and decide for themselves whether they want to continue living according to those ideas.

Nature became another means of expressing what is happening inside the household. The main house has extensive glass surfaces, meaning that leaves and other natural movement are constantly visible behind the characters. Takenoshin initially found this useful for creating continuity and flow between scenes, but gradually began thinking of nature as a larger force surrounding the family. Since their separation feels increasingly inevitable, the environment creates an impression that something larger is pushing them toward a destination they may be unable to avoid. The fireball functions similarly as an unexplained, almost supernatural presence.

Despite being the director, Takenoshin did not approach the production as though he needed to establish himself as “the man in charge”. He was the youngest person on set in terms of professional experience, even though some of the young actors were younger in age, having already worked in the industry since childhood. What allowed him to function comfortably was the collaborative atmosphere created around the production. Once filming began, he no longer felt particularly conscious of being the least experienced person there.

The extensive silence in “Hinotama” developed naturally from Takenoshin’s writing and preparation process. His first screenplay drafts tend to contain a great deal of dialogue. Once locations and actors are established, however, he begins constructing shots and often realizes that dialogue can be replaced by a camera movement, a person crossing a room or simply the relationship between bodies and space. The original screenplay ran approximately 130 pages, but after he spent around a week living inside the house where the film would be shot, it had fallen to about 110, with much of the missing material consisting of dialogue.

That interest in space is closely connected to his cinematic influences. Michael Haneke and Michelangelo Antonioni were particularly important when Takenoshin was younger, especially in teaching him how to organize figures within a frame and use architecture dramatically. However, when he initially tried to reproduce their formal qualities in his college films, he found that his own work became excessively cold and dry. He subsequently began looking toward filmmakers whose work, in his view, contained a stronger human element.

Ryusuke Hamaguchi became particularly important in that respect and remains one of Takenoshin’s major cinematic heroes, while Eric Rohmer is another favorite. The challenge for “Hinotama” was therefore not simply to construct carefully controlled compositions, but to find a way for formal precision and human emotion to coexist.

The house itself helped determine much of the cinematography. Its large windows and strongly geometric architecture immediately attracted Takenoshin, who noticed the abundance of straight lines and ordered spaces. Those characteristics could visually reflect both the father’s insistence on particular forms of behavior and the broader sense of suppression inside the household. The windows also allowed the camera to occupy a variety of positions while retaining connections between the interiors and the natural world outside.

Finding such a location was partly fortunate. The building had previously operated as a café but was no longer being used, while its owners lived elsewhere. This gave the production access to an interesting architectural space without having to displace residents for a month or rely on a comparatively expensive and visually less distinctive studio house. More importantly, it allowed Takenoshin to actually live there before filming and understand how people might move through it.

Casting the younger characters was done through auditions, while most of the adult roles were offered directly. Takenoshin first selected the actor playing Takeshi and then organized the rest of the younger cast around him. What immediately attracted him was the difficulty of reading the young actor’s face. There was an opacity to his expression that suggested something was happening internally without revealing exactly what, a quality Takenoshin compares with actors such as Alain Delon and Kyle MacLachlan.

Takenoshin’s own filmmaking journey began unusually early. At 16, he started making documentaries about nuclear power, motivated initially more by an interest in nuclear energy than cinema. After the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, he had become fascinated by how polarized discussions surrounding the subject were and thought documentary might provide a means of communicating across those divisions. Over approximately three years and two documentaries, however, his interest gradually shifted. Shooting, editing and studying films became increasingly compelling until filmmaking itself overtook nuclear energy as his central concern.

Getting “Hinotama” made involved another unlikely development. Takenoshin wrote the screenplay during his junior year of college and originally imagined shooting it with a very small student crew. Unsure how even a basic feature production should be budgeted and scheduled, he contacted an established cinematographer Yoshio Kitagawa, through Instagram simply to ask practical questions. After they met for coffee, Takenoshin gave him the screenplay in the hope of receiving some comments. Around two weeks later, the cinematographer called and told him that he wanted to make the film. He subsequently helped connect Takenoshin with the producer who would bring the project together.

Post-production remained suitably modest. Takenoshin edited “Hinotama” in his bedroom using two monitors his mother borrowed from her office. The first cut took roughly two or three months. Composer Gabriel Brady, a friend from college who had scored all of Takenoshin’s previous films, came to Japan and worked in the same small room, allowing editing and music to develop almost simultaneously through constant conversation.

The film’s silences also reflect Takenoshin’s observations of communication within Japanese families. Conflict does not necessarily involve people continually shouting or explaining what is wrong. He describes Japanese communication as frequently passive-aggressive, with frustration remaining beneath the surface instead of being confronted directly. Too much dialogue or constant sound would have weakened the atmosphere of quiet suppression he wanted to maintain. …

That does not mean Takenoshin considers “Hinotama” an attack on the family itself. He points toward Japan’s long tradition of family cinema, particularly Yasujiro Ozu, whose films neither condemn nor romanticize the institution but instead record its structures, etiquette and changing values. Takenoshin hopes “Hinotama” can function in a similar way: a personal story that also records something recognizable about the contemporary Japanese family and, eventually, the particular period in which it was made.

Takenoshin is already writing new scripts, although he is not yet ready to discuss them. For now, “Hinotama: Ball of Fire” represents the culmination of a journey that began with teenage documentaries and developed through film study, chance encounters and a highly collaborative first feature. Its combination of controlled space, silence, nature and fantasy suggests a filmmaker interested not in telling audiences exactly what is wrong with his characters, but in placing familiar behavior inside a frame and allowing us to finally notice it.
